title: Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian: How the Greek and Roman Orders Differ
description: Learn to tell Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns apart, how Greek and Roman architects used them differently, and where to spot each order today.
body_html:
The fastest way to tell the three classical orders apart is to look at the capital, the decorated block at the top of the column. A Doric capital is a plain cushion, an Ionic capital has two rolled scrolls called volutes, and a Corinthian capital is a basket of carved acanthus leaves. Greek architects treated these orders as complete design systems governing proportion and ornament from base to roofline; Roman architects inherited them, loosened the rules, added variations of their own, and applied the orders decoratively to arched and vaulted buildings the Greeks never built.

That one-paragraph answer will get you through most trivia nights. The fuller story, below, will let you read almost any courthouse, bank, or museum facade you walk past.

The Three Orders at a Glance

FeatureDoricIonicCorinthian
CapitalPlain rounded cushion under a square slabPaired spiral volutesCarved acanthus leaves with small corner scrolls
ProportionsStockiest; sturdy and muscularSlimmer and more gracefulSlimmest and tallest of the three
BaseNone in the Greek version; sits directly on the platformStacked rings of moldingsMolded base, similar to Ionic
FriezeAlternating triglyphs (grooved blocks) and metopes (panels)Continuous band, often sculptedContinuous band, often richly sculpted
Traditional characterMasculine, severeElegant, scholarlyOrnate, festive
Famous ancient exampleParthenon, AthensErechtheion, AthensTemple of Olympian Zeus, Athens; widely used across Rome

A Quick Vocabulary of the Classical Column

A few terms make the rest of this guide easier to follow. The shaft is the vertical body of the column, sometimes carved with vertical grooves called flutes. The capital is the decorated top; the base, when present, is the stack of moldings at the bottom. Above the columns runs the entablature, a horizontal beam zone divided into three bands: the architrave at the bottom, the frieze in the middle, and the projecting cornice on top. On a temple front, the triangular gable above the entablature is the pediment. Two more terms you will meet on modern buildings: a pilaster is a flattened column projecting slightly from a wall, purely decorative, and a colonnade is a row of columns carrying an entablature. Each order defines a coordinated design for all of these parts, which is why identifying one element usually predicts the rest.

Doric: The Sturdy Original

Doric is the oldest and plainest of the three. Greek Doric columns are broad relative to their height, carved with shallow vertical grooves called flutes that meet in sharp edges, and famously stand without a base, rising straight from the temple platform. Above the columns, the Doric entablature carries its signature frieze of triglyphs and metopes, a rhythm thought to echo the beam ends of earlier timber construction. The order reads as strength, which is why the Greeks used it for their most monumental temples and why it still shows up on buildings that want to project stability.

Roman Doric is easy to confuse with its Greek parent but differs in telling ways: Roman versions are slimmer, usually stand on a base, and often have unfluted shafts. The Romans also developed the closely related Tuscan order, a stripped-down Doric cousin with a smooth shaft and simple moldings.

Ionic: Scrolls and Refinement

Ionic developed in the Greek cities of the eastern Aegean and reads as lighter and more elegant. The giveaway is the capital's pair of volutes, which look like a partly unrolled scroll or, less reverently, a ram's horns. Ionic columns are taller for their width than Doric, carry more flutes separated by flat fillets rather than sharp edges, and always stand on a molded base. The frieze above runs as a continuous band, which gave sculptors room for processions and narrative scenes.

One quirk worth knowing: a classic Ionic capital has a front and a back, since the scrolls face outward in one direction. Corner columns forced awkward compromises, and later designers often used a variant with volutes angled to face both ways.

Corinthian: The Leafy Showpiece

Corinthian is essentially an Ionic column wearing a more elaborate crown. Its capital wraps two staggered rows of stylized acanthus leaves around a bell-shaped core, with small volutes curling out at the corners. It is the tallest and most slender order, and by far the most expensive to carve, which is exactly why patrons loved it. The Greeks invented it late and used it sparingly, mostly for interiors and small monuments. It took the Romans to make Corinthian the default order of empire.

How Greek and Roman Usage Differed

The deepest difference is not in the columns themselves but in how each culture deployed them:

  • Structure versus decoration. Greek architecture is post-and-lintel: columns genuinely hold the building up, so the order is the structure. Roman engineering ran on the arch, the vault, and concrete, so columns frequently became engaged (half-embedded in the wall) or purely ornamental, framing arches they did not support. The Colosseum's stacked arcades, with a different order applied at each level, are the textbook case.
  • Order preferences. The Greeks favored Doric and Ionic, reserving Corinthian for special uses. The Romans overwhelmingly preferred Corinthian for temples and public monuments, prizing its richness.
  • New orders. Rome added the plain Tuscan order and the Composite order, which stacks Ionic volutes on top of a Corinthian leaf basket, giving a canonical set of five orders that Renaissance writers later codified.
  • Pedestals and podiums. Greek temples sat on a stepped platform accessible from all sides; Roman temples typically stood on a high podium with a single frontal stair, and Roman columns often rose from pedestals.
  • Rule-following. Greek designers refined each order with subtle optical corrections, such as columns that swell slightly and lean inward. Roman practice, transmitted through the writer Vitruvius, was more standardized but also more freely mixed, happily combining orders, arches, and domes in one building.

Spotting the Orders on Modern Buildings

The classical orders never really went away. They returned in force in Neoclassical architecture from the eighteenth century onward, and again in the grand civic buildings of the Beaux-Arts era. When you pass a courthouse, capitol, bank, museum, or university library with a columned portico, run the checklist:

  1. Look at the capital first. Cushion means Doric or Tuscan, scrolls mean Ionic, leaves mean Corinthian, and leaves plus large scrolls mean Composite.
  2. Check the shaft. Fluted shafts lean Greek-inspired; smooth shafts suggest Roman or Tuscan influence.
  3. Check the base. No base at all is a strong signal of Greek Revival Doric.
  4. Read the frieze. Triglyphs confirm Doric; a continuous or sculpted band points to Ionic or Corinthian.
  5. Note the context. Government buildings often chose Doric or Ionic for gravitas, while banks, theaters, and monuments frequently splurged on Corinthian.

Interpretation matters as much as identification. A nineteenth-century American courthouse with baseless fluted Doric columns is quoting Athenian democracy on purpose, while a domed capitol ringed with Corinthian columns is speaking the architectural language of imperial Rome. Practice Makes Perfect

The orders reward field practice: after a dozen deliberate identifications, the distinctions become instant.
